MR. KORCHINSKI-DENIAL OF INFORMATION TO HOUSE ON PROPOSED TWO-PRICE SYSTEM FOR WHEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise a question of privilege affecting the rights of all hon. members. It concerns the contempt for parliament of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) as indicated by his refusal to provide information on the so-called two-price system for wheat while continuing to provide the media with information which, if it so suited the minister, could be denied as not factual.
On February 21 in reply to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) the Minister of Justice who is in charge of the Wheat Board, stated that various methods of payment and timing were being considered by the government. I followed through with a question on that day and the minister replied as follows:
All these questions are really linked together and require an announcement of policy in connection with timing and the technique of making payments. Such an announcement will deal with all these matters at the same time.
I find that the minister has since made an announcement on the method of payment. It is found in Canadian Press and Southam Press reports in various Saturday papers. I suggest that this is contempt of Parliament. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie):
That the matter of the growing disregard by the government for the right of this House to information on public business through the channels provided by the procedures of this House be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. KORCHINSKI-DENIAL OF INFORMATION TO HOUSE ON PROPOSED TWO-PRICE SYSTEM FOR WHEAT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Mackenzie has supplied the Chair with the required notice of his intention to raise this matter by way of a question of privilege.
The hon. member suggests that the matter to which he has alluded in his statement ought to be considered by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. I have to rule that this cannot be done under the terms of our Standing Orders.
As the hon. member knows, and as I am sure all members appreciate, from time to time there have been grievances brought to the attention of the House along the same lines, suggestions that statements not made in the House were made outside the House, or that information not given to members in reply to questions was supplied to the media or in some other way given outside the House. There is a long line of learned rulings, going back many years, indicating that this is more a grievance than a breach of privilege, that it could be the subject of
debate, that it might be the subject of a censure motion, that it could be the subject of a grievance, but that it could not be considered as suggested in the motion proposed by the hon. member for Mackenzie.

REASONS FOR REMISSION OF SALES TAX TO GREAT CANADIAN OIL SANDS LIMITED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance who appears to think he is still Minister of Justice. Some days ago I inquired of the President of the Treasury Board about the remission of $6 million to Great Canadian Oil Sands Limited by Order in Council pursuant, it was said in the order, to section 17 of the Financial Administration Act. The last time I asked the question the President of the Treasury Board said that the Minister of Finance would inform the House of the basis on which that generous remission of money to a company was made.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: REASONS FOR REMISSION OF SALES TAX TO GREAT CANADIAN OIL SANDS LIMITED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand that my predecessor has already made a statement on this matter outside the House. However, to answer formally in the House the question put to the President of the Treasury Board by the hon. member for York South, may I say I have looked into the matter and have to report that feasibility studies, planning and preparation for this major project of building and equipment by Great Canadian Oil Sands to extract oil from the Alberta tar sands, were completed before the sales tax was first imposed on June 14, 1963. Construction of the plant was not completed and production did not commence until after June 2, 1967, when production equipment was again exempted from the sales tax. The company has incurred serious financial losses since the outset of production and therefore sought remission of sales tax which had not applied when their plans were being drawn up and was later withdrawn across the country after the plant was finished. Although the company sought remission of all federal sales tax on buildings, plant and equipment, remission was granted only in respect of production equipment.

subtopic: REASONS FOR REMISSION OF SALES TAX TO GREAT CANADIAN OIL SANDS LIMITED
speechtext:
As I understand it, the Financial Administration Act provides that the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board, whenever he

considers it in the public interest may remit any tax, fee or penalty. Would the Minister of Finance indicate briefly to the House what public interest, aside from the interest of a corporation that had some argument, was served to justify the government taking steps under the Financial Administration Act to remit $6 million to a single company, and would that be available to an individual taxpayer who suffered the same kind of hardship?

subtopic: REASONS FOR REMISSION OF SALES TAX TO GREAT CANADIAN OIL SANDS LIMITED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member knows that remission is given under the Financial Administration Act from time to time and that it is not unusual. He has asked what special circumstances existed here. I said that the sales tax had not originally applied when the plans and feasibility studies for the plant were drawn up and construction commenced, and by the time the plant had been completed and production had begun the sales tax was off. I think that probably in the mind of the government at the time the public interest involved a major pioneer project for extracting oil from the Alberta tar sands, something which may be invaluable to this country in the years ahead.

subtopic: REASONS FOR REMISSION OF SALES TAX TO GREAT CANADIAN OIL SANDS LIMITED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not ask the minister what special circumstances there were, because the act does not talk about special circumstances. Is that the way the government interprets the public interest, the remission of public money to a single corporation?

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, February 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ross Whicher for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session and the amendment thereto of Mr. Alexander (p. 212).

Mr. ]ean-L. Rochon (Ahuntsic): Mr. Speaker, I have listened very attentively to the remarks made since the opening of this session by all those who contributed to the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
According to their political affiliation, some have approved it without any reservation whatsoever; others found it incomplete and many, without disapproving it completely, would have liked to see in it a clearer expression of the feelings they have toward those they represent in the House. If you look more closely, however, you realize-for this is very obvious-that all members, whether of the opposition or the government party, are animated with the same feeling: the same clear and unfailing desire, the same unequivocal determination to contribute to the well-being of Canadians.
Last December, addressing the whole world at Christmas, Pope Paul VI spoke in a way which must have made many people think in the days we live in, when our world is shaken by all kinds of crises, by civil and religious strife-a world which struggles with hardly any hope for the future because of hunger and the diseases which it causes and which turn people into human wrecks who can be freed by death only.
Those words of the Holy Father have given this world a glimmer of hope. We used to say-in my generation at least-when we were studying classics: "If you want peace, prepare war". But in our day of social unrest, of bloody strife, a voice rose to say to the world: "If you want peace, prepare justice".
Mr. Speaker, I will not be accused of exaggerating if I maintain that the action of this government, which I am proud to support, is to a large extent aimed in that direction. To be convinced of this-and in spite of what our opponents may say-one only has to look at both this government's past efforts and accomplishments and the plans for the future which it announces in the Speech from the Throne.
As far as I know, Mr. Speaker, we do not have a complete record of all the speeches made since 1867. Such a compilation would be interesting for various reasons, if only to provide a summary, so to speak, of the preoccupations of the various governments which have been in office over slightly more than a century.
Surely one thing would be obvious. One hundred years ago, those in power did not seem excessively social-minded. The way of thinking that prevailed in those days made them more trade-oriented than anything else. Their concern was more directed toward ensuring the wealth of the country in general or of the propertied class than that of the other sectors of society.

February 28, 1972
Speech from the Throne
Our fathers did not take exception to differences in fortune which were much more shocking than presently. The government did not think of establishing a just society as this would have been considered if not strange at least unattainable.
However, it must be recognized that a century ago the poor adjusted themselves to their condition more readily than currently. Times have changed and the political history of the last 50 years is that of a slow emergence of what we might call the social concept.
More and more all our governments have given priority to these questions and legislation passed within the last few years bears witness to that. But this is a complex area and the search for justice, by its very nature, is an ever-recurring and never-completed operation.
Of course we can see actual progress but this will never correspond, whatever we do, to total and final success. But in this field, as in many others, you need not hope to undertake and need not succeed to persevere. Allow me to refer to the Speech from the Throne which we are currently debating, and I quote:
In a period dominated by bigness, in an increasingly impersonal social system, one of the major challenges facing government is to remove the impression of isolation which so often surrounds men and women, depriving them of their sense of worth, of accomplishment, of fulfilment, and removing from them their identity as individuals.
This feeling of isolation, or to quote a fashionable expression widely used nowadays, of alienation is probably a new phenomenon. If we go back to the post-war years, when another liberal government laid the foundations of the social security program-one of the most comprehensive in the world-we enjoy today, we have the impression that our predecessors were sincerely convinced that a better distribution of wealth, while insuring that the underprivileged would be, as far as practicable, shielded from misery, would have simultaneously eradicated the deep root causes of social unrest.
But what is happening? We have noted that more than 25 years of relative peace and a quarter century of almost uninterrupted economic progress have not solved a great deal. We did not find it enough for us to guarantee to the economically weak the social benefits that would, at the same time, solve the problem of poverty. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the word "poor" is almost new in our political jargon. When I was first elected to this House in 1962, it was hardly uttered. Now almost everyone mentions it, which is an indication, I think, that we are now conscious of the fact that it is not enough for a country to tackle the problems of its poors, but that it should strive to redeem their human dignity.
This is the political trend of the present government. Urgent economic necessities related, for instance, to defending, in the public interest, the integrity of our currency and the comprehensive review of our fiscal policy, should not be construed as a sign, even temporary, of negligence toward our social calling but, on the contrary, as the implementation of measures to reach that goal. In this regard, long excerpts from the Speech from the Throne could be quoted.
New national parks, the fight against unemployment, a better economic climate, the maintenance of stable prices,

there are measures in which we must see as many aspects of a social policy, in its widest but also in its truest sense.
Mr. Speaker, the government was accused of encouraging unemployment in its fight against inflation. That accusation dishonours those who cast it. We may perhaps have achieved more success in the first instance than in the second. Price increases, in Canada, rank among the lowest recorded in the industrial countries of the world. This remarkable feat, for which the government should be congratulated, was of benefit to all citizens.
Inflation, Mr. Speaker, is a deeply rooted and demoralizing evil whose spreading effects spare no one. Unemployment is a more apparent scourge, more easily definable but surely terrible for its victims. However, experience has shown us that it is of a more temporary nature and that its effects are less protracted. We have already noted some improvement in that respect this winter in comparison with last winter and no doubt that through the economic incentive program which we have undertaken, it will be possible to lessen those effects, thanks especially to the new provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I have spoken about the tax reform, the fight against inflation and unemployment but I could deal at length with many other aspects of the government's administration. It is not exaggerated to say that Canada has led the way by taking various steps to protect the environment. Ours is one of the few countries with a Department of the Environment specially vested with this responsibility. However, even before the department was set up, we had already taken a great many measures to protect the purity of air, water and soil, such as the Clean Air Act, the ban on DDT and phosphates, the Canada Water Act, all measures introduced by this government and reflecting this vitally social concern.
We implemented the Opportunities for Youth program. We instituted studies on drugs, the results of which are now taking concrete legislative form. We created Manpower Centres specially geared to students, etc. Although this aspect of the government's activities may have given rise to criticisms, on the whole we can claim real achievements. We have also taken many steps to protect farmers, to defend the interests of the consumer and to broaden Canadian international action.
In almost every case, I will point out, we have had to do without the support of the opposition, for adoption of legislation on the marketing of farm products, for fiscal reform and many other measures which were required in Canada.
I shall now stop my enumeration of the various beneficial measures passed and implemented by a government which has demonstrated more concern with serving the best interests of the nation than with ensuring its popularity. It is true that, the more courage we have shown, the more hostility we have incurred from both labour and business circles. The fact that so many private interests have felt aggrieved confirms our feeling that we have protected the public interest.
Apart from all such matters, the Speech from the Throne announces truly new legislation. One measure, for instance, concerning up-to-date and flexible competition will not please everybody, but will be of benefit to our
February 28, 1972

country. New provisions with regard to income security may appear too generous to some, insufficient to others, but no matter, it is the general good that is sought.
Even though Canada may have more quality housing starts than almost all other countries in the world, it will always be said that it is not enough. This government has chosen to do its duty, all of its duty. Accordingly, it deserves to be encouraged and congratulated. Things cannot always be perfect. The government accepts criticism, but this criticism must be constructive. It will have been noted, doubtless, that since the beginning of this session, for lack of more serious subjects, the opposition refers only to issues such as the Geoffroy case or the alleged intention of removing the term "Royal" from the designation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), toward the end of last week, ansered these accusations as he was touring northern Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, I would rather not linger too long on this subject, but I can asy that the government's achievements arouse little enthusiasm on our opponents' part. This is understandable. It is even understandable that a certain part of the press, confusing the right to criticize with the duty to criticize, did not aspare it its reproaches. Fortunately, Canada has more objective and detached observers.
Reviewing, much as I have just done, the action of the government for the past few years, the Journal de Montreal on February 14 last published an article which stated in part:
In these particularly difficult times, the government remains vigilant and active. It was able to solve problems overcome crises and it works more than ever to improve the living conditions of all Canadians.
It could not be stated better. But if the value of this evidence is suspected, perhaps one will be more impressed by that of Le Devoir, a paper which is not very sympathetic to the government, as is well known. In an article by its Ottawa correspondent who also reviewed the legislative action of the government, it was stated in conclusion:
The government ensured the passing of many reformist acts of great importance, including the monumental tax reform bill and it succeeded as never before in keeping the attention of Canadians focussed on the central parliamentary institution.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that some measure of parliamentary reform, vehemently opposed by the opposition, will ensure that Parliament will now be able to act faster and better in the numerous fields in which it has to take action.
Nevertheless there is some contradiction in the fact that the very people who never stop asking that the government interfere in everything are not very competent themselves. Indeed, they spend their time reproaching the government with its slowness, its mismanagement and its idleness. But those are the very people who resist the most vehemently all attempts made by Parliament to facilitate sensible discussion of measures that often are vital for the public interest. The Canadian people are not taken in by that ambiguity and they will not believe that the government has trampled down the rights of Parliament, if I may use an expression often used by hon. members of the opposition. On the contrary, they are grateful to it for
Speech from the Throne
having taken measures to allow the representatives of the people to express themselves in an absolutely democratic way, that is in giving them the opportunity to take a vote on the proposals submitted to them.
Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss if I did not, like previous speakers, pay tribute to the hon. member who moved the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, as well as to the seconder. Both deserve much from their country. They have shown themselves worthy of the confidence which their electors had put in them, and I am convinced that both realize that a brilliant future lies afead of them.
To end these few remarks, may I, Mr. Speaker, call on all members of the opposition or the government to work together hand in hand. Let us work for the increased well-being of this country, and instead of condemning everything, sowing hatred, as some are trying to do, let us co-operate. As for those who would criticize us and try to get ahead by destroying reputations, may I remind them that "He who sows the wind shall reap the whirlwind".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I participate in a Throne Speech debate for the first time, even though I have sat here as a member for six years and would like to think that I may sit here longer although that will be left to the electorate in the not too distant future, I suppose, I enter the debate with two basic thoughts that I want to present to the House. I believe they underline part of the problem in Canada, and in a philosophical way I have entitled them "The Paradoxes of the Prime Minister".
After listening to the last speaker refer to criticism and then immediately talk about hate, and accepting the sincerity of the views he expressed, I hope that no one after listening to what I have to say will suggest that one can equate criticism, either constructive or negative, if one can divide criticism in that semantic form, with any hint of hate, prejudice or bigotry.
As I sit as a Member of Parliament and hear questions concerning Canada discussed, our constitution, the monarchy and our parliamentary form of government, and then on television see the problems which exist to the south of us, I believe that those to the south of us at times have more to be thankful for than we in this country. Although they have problems and divisions I personally believe there is more frank discussion of those problems. Sides are taken passionately in an effort to solve their dilemma. We in Canada have a character blended from the two founding races with an infusion of the blood of many other peoples. We always seem to opt for compromise, for the easy way out, and avoid the basic issues confronting the land.
When the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) ascended the throne, so to speak, assumed the mantle of leadership of his party and fought an election, he appeared to speak frankly and realistically about the problems that face Canada. His frankness was stimulating. I believe there was hope in all parties and certainly among many of the younger people of Canada. People felt that at last,

February 28, 1972
Speech from the Throne
although the fundamental problems of this land would not be solved overnight-after all, no one party has a monopoly on solving our basic dilemmas-we were beginning to talk frankly and freely about our problems and we might attempt to resolve those problems in that spirit while recognizing at the same time the fundamental differences that have permeated the Canadian fabric for the past 100 years. Change is possible. Consider what has happened recently. President Nixon, a former communist baiter, has been honoured in Peking. He has been eating pheasant, duck and all those other delicacies available there.
Our forefathers, among whom I include Sir John A. Macdonald, were men of fundamentally diverse views but they got together and settled their differences. Those differences were based on philosophy, religion and origin and aroused greater discord than they might today when we have been emancipated by so-called education and technology. I wonder if there has ever been a political leader in this land who has evoked such an image as a young man who was adventurous and ready to experiment with new ways. If the President of the United States can change his anti-red posture and take the sort of trip he has taken to China, why should the people of this country not be able to sink their differences. However, we in Canada, I am afraid, are not prepared to sit down together frankly and discuss points of difference in the hope of bridging those differences and arriving at a consensus on what is best for Canada.
If there is anything that disenchants me about the four years that the present Prime Minister has been in office it is, if we forget for the moment unemployment and inflation, that during those four years that frankness and realism in approaching our difficulties which we had expected was never apparent. To me, Mr. Speaker, this involves a paradox. I doubt whether any man in recent times has come up so suddenly and so soon, stimulated such warmth, such excitement and radiated such charisma and yet, after attaining office, has become so cool, aloof and distant. In place of the former charisma we now see coolness and distance. In attempting to deal with today's problems the Prime Minister did not seem to be merely in an intellectual ivory tower; he seemed to be almost in an intellectual igloo. He has not cared about the plight of thousands of Canadians confronted with the reality of unemployment and caught in the squeeze of ever-spiralling inflation.
I will be the first to admit that no government will solve these difficulties overnight. Nevertheless, we must face the paradox of a Prime Minister who, having shown warmth and compassion before election, seemed at times to lose the capacity to feel compassion after his election. I believe that a Prime Minister of this country cannot solve the country's problems involving confederation unless he brings to the study of those problems a great degree of care and compassion. In approaching solutions he must not deal with the problem as though it is like a tangent of a circle in a geometric plane; neither should he imagine that you can feed figures into a computer and obtain a programmed result. Problems involving people cannot be solved by computers or braintrusts alone, although these can help in providing the options available. You need the human element. Human beings must make the ultimate

decisions if we are to produce results which, although they may not satisfy everyone, will at least meet the approval of most.
Apart from the contrast displayed by the Prime Minister's attitude of warmth and concern on the one hand and coolness, detachment and an "I don't care" attitude on the other, we must also consider some of the things the Prime Minister has said, and especially the names he has called the premiers of certain provinces. Your Honour is well aware that, if we are to judge from the heat engendered in this chamber when some hon. members have called others names, name-calling on a national scale can bring about the breakdown of our system of government. The whole thing could break down. Think of what happens in this chamber when there is name-calling and imputation of motives. I say, why does the man who sits in the most responsible chair of the land, the Prime Minister's chair, not exercise greater responsibility in describing his feelings with regard to some of the leaders of this land? This is another example of the "I care and I don't care" attitude, of this warm-cool paradox I have spoken about.
Four years ago the Prime Minister was elected under a one-Canada banner, and a very attractive banner it was, too, pulling at the heart-strings of the nation. It is ironic that four years later there should be more discontent, disillusionment and disenchantment between the peoples of the various regions of this country than there has been for some time.
One reason for this breakdown in the common will, for this deterioration in our national fibre and fabric, and for the polarization between the various regions of this country, a polarization which is just beginning, is that for the first time there is in cabinet a group which, ironically, is not involved in national participation. I will not go into name-calling and say that there is in cabinet a Montreal Mafia and that there are three of four men who wield power while others, even cabinet ministers, must knock on the door. That has been said many times, and there is a good deal of truth to it. You need only look at the estimates for this year-I will go into those in greater detail soon-to realize who are the Midas twins and where the money is going. Much money is going to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Much is going to the department headed by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) and those agencies for which he is responsible. As for the Secretary of State, and I am glad to see him in the House because I intend to say more about his department, there has been an attraction of agencies and a compounding of dollars under his administration that make other ministries seem rather small indeed. These ministers are the Midas twins. It must be a compliment to their competence and aggressive nature, let alone any other factors, that they administer the two most active, sometimes imaginative and certainly the largest departments in the sense of new programs, not statutory matters which are built into the budget such as health and welfare. However, they are not voices for Canada as a whole in helping to develop a consensus in the cabinet. In fact, the development of a consensus springs too much from the basic center of this land-some might suggest only from Montreal or Quebec.
February 28, 1972

If we review the ministries we see that, starting with Sir John A. Macdonald, we had a Cartier and a Tupper from Atlantic Canada. Omitting some ministries and coming down to the days of real Liberalism, the man who indelibly stamped his imprint on the Canadian context more than any other one man, certainly in the twentieth century, through some of the programs he initiated and his avoidance of some of the fundamental problems with which we are still grappling-I mention bilingualism as one-was Mackenzie King. Mackenzie King, the Presbyterian and Protestant, had Lapointe, Jimmy Gardiner, Stuart Garson, C. D. Howe and Jimmy Ilsley in his cabinet. These were fine Canadians from various regions of Canada. They brought to the cabinet points of view which were not just confined to the television centres of Toronto and Montreal and did not just come from the geographical context of Ottawa. Whether they liked it or not, they represented a group. They did not come here initially as voices from Saskatchewan or Port Arthur or the voice of business. They brought to cabinet a balance of varying points of view from important ministers, something which is not found in the present cabinet.
The present cabinet, regardless of fuzzy-wuzzy tinkers as a colleague of mine suggested not too long ago, has in terms of actual power a very narrow base that has not been exposed to some of the realities of Canada from coast to coast. There are fine men from British Columbia and Toronto and a very interesting gentleman from Nova Scotia, but under Mackenzie King the President of the Privy Council was closer to the seat of power than under the present Prime Minister. These things come and go. Ministries have men who are close to the Prime Minister and men who are somewhat removed by distance and philosophy and thus the door does not open quite so readily.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) mentions the Minister of Finance. This is the reality of cabinet-making. It will continue under any administration, but the flaw in the present administration is that there is not the dilution of different points of view coming into the common stream.
Mr. Pearson had Jimmy Sinclair who has now attained fame in another way. He brought a responsible point of view from British Columbia. At one time George Mcll-raith used to bring a very definite point of view to cabinet council. He was not only heard but listened to, and there is a big difference between the two. Mr. Pickersgill brought to cabinet a very historical past and a very political present. He certainly added his point of view to cabinet council. There was Mr. Chevrier, an honoured representative of a riding about which Your Honour knows quite a bit. Regardless of political background, these men were of sterling character and brought their points of view to cabinet council. The results of cabinet deliberations were not dictated just because a man happened to be infused with the culture of Toronto or Montreal. There was a balance.
Speech from the Throne
I need only go back to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). He brought a balanced point of view from coast to coast. The lesson of history is remote but, ironically, there was more of a Canadian spark, be it a Canadian vision, Arctic plans or northern development. There was a one-Canadian approach. In his cabinet were Howard Green, Davie Fulton, Gordon Churchill, Hugh John Flemming and many others.

I would like to continue, Mr. Speaker. My whip has informed me that I have only ten more minutes.
I would like to conclude in that time. I have the problem of speaking too long rather than otherwise because I have so much of substance to say, not because I am prolix. I would like to complete my remarks.
We have the one paradox of the man with the warm charisma while campaigning who, following election, becomes the cool inhabitant of an intellectural igloo, a man without compassion who does not care. I suggest in all seriousness that the administration is going to have to combat in the next election the fact that the Prime Minister does not really care about a single problem. The other paradox is that under this ministry-I am not saying there is not regional representation, but that is not what I am talking about-the ministers who have the ear of the Prime Minister and his administration have a very narrow background. I do not mean narrow personally but because of geographic and other interests.
Before I try to dissect some of the estimates of the Secretary of State, I must say there is one thing that appalled me and caught me by surprise, although I should have been aware of it. When we look at this handy book put out by the President of the Treasury Board, which confuses rather than clarifies and hides more than it shows, we see it is shown in clear form that in the six short years since I came here the estimates have more than doubled from $7.2 billion in 1965 to $15.7 billion for 1972-73. We all know this is not the end. In six short years the estimates have more than doubled. Four years ago the present Prime Minister came on the scene with frugality and thrift. Later I will deal with how much his administration has cost. In a cumulative way the four Trudeau years will cost the Canadian taxpayer more than the first 85 years of Canadian federal government in total expenditure. This is the man who is so frugal and thrifty. The figures are clear. I have them here.
Let us talk about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and see what it has done. The time has come for Canadians to take a hard look at the CBC. Personally, I am in favour of a national broadcasting service. However, the proposed expenditures on current account are $207

February 28, 1972
Speech from the Throne
million, not counting the $31 million in loans. Compare this with total federal expenditures of $184.9 million in 1914. Indeed, federal government revenues did not reach the present level of the CBC for this year until the wartime year of 1917.
Look at the Department of Secretary of State. Proposed expenditures amount to more than $1 billion when one counts post-secondary transfer payments of $28 million. Mr. Speaker, total federal government expenditure did not exceed that amount in any year until Canada had been at war with Hitler for two years. To put it in another way, it took the first ten years of confederation for the Canadian Federal government to spend more than the CBC proposes to spend in the next financial year. It took the first 30 years since Confederation for the federal government to spend as much as the Secretary of State proposes to be responsible for spending in the next financial year. It took 49 years of confederation to spend as much as the Secretary of State has spent in four years, that is, $3.2 billion. It took the federal government the first 74 years of confederation to spend as much as the present administration proposes to spend next year. The four Trudeau years will cost Canadian taxpayers more than the first 85 years of federal government.
I ask, without trying to stimulate culture at all, is it any wonder that we should not be surprised, with estimates growing at this rate, with such large amounts set aside for culture at the expense, it would seem, of allocations, to certain practical programs, that the Canadian taxpayer is beginning to wonder where we are heading? If time were available I would go into more detail, though I could not hope to discuss fully the mythology of the hasty handbook for confused Canadians prepared by the President of the Treasury Board.

speechtext:
That is the title. I was not referring personally to any minister. In this publication, purporting to show taxpayers how their dollar is spent, the President of the Treasury Board suggest we are each of us contributing in taxes 2 cents for culture and recreation. This is almost worthy of a question of privilege. One has only to look at the other pages, at the sections in which expenditures on which other programs are buried, to find that instead of two cents being spent on culture the amount is easily between four and five cents. It would be ridiculous if it were not so serious.
We find the estimates relating to The Company of Young Canadians under Health and Welfare. I do not know whose health these people have helped or to whose welfare they have contributed. More interesting to me is the fact that the allocation in respect of translation and bilingual programs, to the tune of $50 million, is to be found under the heading "Internal Overhead Expenditures". I would have thought that if anything were basic to culture it would be expenditure on bilingual programs. Similarly, $90 million proposed for education assistance in the year 1972-73 is found separately listed. Of course, when the work of 29 departments is broken down to 11 functions, expenditures have to be shifted around-there has to be a little shell game-but let us not put all these

items which are related to culture under different headings. The additional expenditures to which I have referred could easily add a further $318 million to the figure of $365 million given us in the little handbook, and I believe I can say this without provoking any debate with the Secretary of State who is responsible for all these programs.
Before closing I should like to deal with one further item here. It concerns translation costs. I believe there is a lot of hocus-pocus in connection with the translation of French into English and English into French. Translation services are, of course, important having regard to the bilingual character of this nation, but I think we have gone overboard. Look at the figures. Between 1961 and 1965, translation cost us $7.7 million. Between 1965 and 1969 the cost was $14.9 million. Four years of this administration, based on the 1969-1973 figures will give rise to translation costs amounting to no less than $41 million, more than is to be expended on northern economic development this year, or even next year, for which the estimate is $38.7 million. The proposed expenditure on translation next year is $15 million compared with $2.7 million for the Economic Council of Canada. I suggest this represents a sad degree of imbalance in the determination of priorities. We are spending $15 million in one year and $15.7 next year on translation while providing $2.7 million in the same period for the functions of the Economic Council, five times as much for translation as a specific subject than for economic planning, and this is at a time when the country badly needs economic planning.
My time has almost expired but there are many more things I could say. I hope to have the opportunity to say them at another time. I believe that as we head down the back stretch-I am referring to the days when I used to run races-on the last lap of this parliament, the government will have to show that it cares. It will have to demonstrate that there is a measure of balance in its decisions. I am not talking now of the Liberal party. The Liberal party is a great and famous institution of the land-too strong as far as I am concerned. On this note I suggest that a government which was capable of approaching decisions in a balanced way would never have involved itself in the little problem which has arisen with respect to the RCMP. It may seem only a small matter but it is large in the eyes of many people. Members opposite can sniff and sneer, but I would point out to them that this difficulty has never risen before. It did not arise during the administration of the previous Solicitor General who was a wise old fox around the corridors of this Hill. This is another thorn which I hope will prick some sensibility, some sensitivity, into the cabinet in order that we may avoid in this land the backlash which could be witnessed unless better judgment is shown.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one or two comments at this time. Some of them will relate to my constituency. But before getting into those subjects I wish to commend the two hon. members who moved and seconded the address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne and join with others who have paid sincere tributes to them. I should like to say how refreshing it was to hear the unabashed, unashamed and enthusiastic views of the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) in a Chamber
February 28, 1972

which is all too often characterized by predictions of disaster, gloom and doom, particularly from the Casan-dras opposite. It was quite refreshing that at least one member of the House could state that government had done something over the past years to justify his saying something positive and enthusiastic about our performance. I only wish that some of this enthusiasm would rub off on members opposite. It is not a question of being smug but simply of recognizing a few facts. During 100 years, this country has achieved certain accomplishments. Perhaps these can be put into some kind of perspective, rather than members dwelling upon some of our shortcomings.
I was intrigued by the contribution made by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan). I too have read "How Your Tax Dollar Is Spent". I did not find it confusing, but I must admit that, after listening to him telling the House that he had read it, I am prepared to believe that it must have been a confusing document to him. I say that because no member of this House, having read that document, could have come forward with such a jumble of ideas so confusedly presented without giving some credence to the claim that the document itself is confusing. I shall re-read it myself and perhaps I shall become as confused as he; but certainly on first reading it did not seem to me confusing but, rather, quite helpful.
The hon. member for Annapolis Valley started to talk about what he called the "two Midases from Quebec". He was, of course, referring to two ministers, one being the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) and the other the minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand). He went on to say that somehow their budgets had been increased. But why did the hon. member devote such a great portion of his speech to talking about increases in budgets? Was he as concerned about the increase in the budget of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion? No, he simply avoided that. The hon. member for Annapolis Valley could not justify, nor could any other member from the Maritimes justify, coming to this House to complain about the increase in the budget of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. So in that selective way that is the trademark of hon. members opposite, the hon. member dealt with but one budget that he felt he could legitimately make some point about, coming from Annapolis Valley.

speechtext:
I want to continue from the point at which I left off at one o'clock and get into the substance of what I want to say. First of all I want to deal with the contribution of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). I will make some comments about what I feel our strategy should be. First of all, I would like to wish him well in what is obviously a difficult portfolio. He has demonstrated an extraordinarily high level of talent in his previous undertakings for this government, and I am sure he will bring these considerable talents to bear successfully in the portfolio he presently holds. In his first speech to the House he wisely warned us, and the public at large, against any false hopes for uninterrupted smooth sailing. Although the economy is strong, despite the gloomy predictions of the Cassandras opposite, there are serious and unresolved problem areas. In his remarks the minister pointed out some of these.
First, there is the highly imperfect and incomplete state of the so called science of economics, where theorists are more noted for their disagreements than for what they agree upon. Second, there is the lack of solid understanding about the phenomenon of cost-push inflation, and the understandable but frustrating lack of consensus on how to deal with this matter. The minister, in his remarks, stated:
Cost-push inflation has frequently occurred to some extent in the past, but more recently it has taken a far more virulent form.
The remedy for the problem most often proposed by Canadians generally is, of course, wage and price controls. The Chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission, Dr. John Young, has indicated that the Commission has studied this matter and has a formula which could be used if there is not successful voluntary restraint. I, for one, would like to see some of the findings of the Commis-

sion made public so that we could examine this matter dispassionately. I note in passing, though, that the Senate Committee on Prices and Incomes reviewed the matter of wage and price controls, invited a series of the most distinguished economists in this country and abroad to advise the committee on the matter and, after their exhaustive study, came out against wage and price controls.
Third, there are the dangers inherent to a trading country like Canada in the formation of trading blocs all around us, particularly trading blocs which have a tendency to be protectionist. Fourth, there is the threat posed to Canadian secondary manufacturers by the brazen plan of export subsidy that the U.S. Congress is allowing through the formation of the Domestic International Sales Corporation, creating a substantial threat to employment in Canada. Fifth, the minister pointed out something which we all too often forget, namely, the pure vagaries of a relatively free market economy operating on the basis of decisions by millions of individuals.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is a further threat to employment levels and to the economy of Canada which was not mentioned by the minister. It is the new, potentially troubling threat to Canadian jobs looming on the U.S. horizon in the form of the Hartke-Burke bill. This bill is supported by the AFL-CIO, and is designed to cut back on imports from abroad. Canada would be the country most affected if this bill, which has been referred to the U.S. Senate Finance Committee, ever became law. This bill would establish a new agency with strong powers to regulate imports. The bill would force Canada to put quotas on its exports to the United States, rolling them back to the average level of exports for the period 1965-69. This bill is being supported by the heads of international unions in the United States. It is a short-sighted, selfish, protectionist measure.
But the irony is that Canadian workers who are members of the same international unions in question will be thrown out of work by the lobbying of the leaders of the unions of which they are members. I think it is important to know what the Canadian heads of the international affiliates of these unions are doing, what pressures they are applying to their counterparts in the United States to stop the progress of this bill. I would also like to know what that political party the NDP, which is nothing more or less than the handmaiden of organized labour in Canada is doing to bring pressure to bear in order to stop this bill.
These are some of the realities with which the Minister of Finance has to contend. His task will not be easy. Recognizing this, perhaps he will forgive me if I chide him gently for what appears to have been somewhat rosy statements about the employment prospects for Canadian workers. I share his view that our first priority must be to provide good jobs for Canadians who are seeking work. That is fair and commendable. I completely endorse that priority. But really, Mr. Speaker, what are the prospects of that priority ever being anything more than a priority?
I don't believe that this government, or in fact any other government can accomplish that goal, and I do not believe that we should leave the impression in the minds of Canadians that it is something that can be done, or done easily.
February 28, 1972

I was disturbed to receive today the first mailing of a document which apparently is the result of an organized campaign in support of "a full employment program."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Are you against full employment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If the hon. member will wait for a second or two he will hear my misgivings about this. What is the program proposed? I quote from the document:
I urge your support demanding this government pass full employment legislation now guaranteeing all Canadians, able and willing to work, jobs at fair wages-
Whatever that means.
-commensurate with their ability or training.
If any political party in this House has such a program, Mr. Speaker, it should produce it. But certainly neither the NDP nor the Conservatives, nor indeed this party, has such a program. I think we should stop trying to leave the impression in the minds of Canadians that somehow there is a simple, miraculous solution, that if this or that group were in power everybody in the country would be fully employed and working at fair wages. I may say that a decision on the last statement would be a rather subjective judgment. Is it to be left to the individual to decide what he is worth? In fact, some people doing our work, Mr. Speaker, think that our wages are too low. We cannot possibly reach that goal.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If the hon. member is so naive that he does not understand this, then I will talk to him privately later. If anyone can point out to me a year when there was full employment in this country, or if the hon. member's colleagues opposite, whose political party was in power for 17 years in Saskatchewan, can point out one year there, or even a full 24 hours when there was full employment at fair wages, then I will retract my statement. But they know perfectly well that they cannot do that. It is pure hypocrisy on their part to suggest that it can be done.
I certainly think that our goal should be to maximize employment, and we can confess to this frankly, but we should also be examining ways in which unemployed and unemployable people can still be active and occupied, alternating between jobs. Our traditional ways of looking at this question have been superseded by events. The high technology industrial state raises new problems and new possibilities. Obviously, there will be less work and more leisure.
Obviously, things like overtime will have to be eliminated. Obviously the 40 hour work-week is becoming redundant in terms of present technology. All these are things that will have to be reviewed, and until they are reviewed we should stop promising full employment. We should begin to think of how we can make periods of unemployment as creative and active as possible. We must start thinking of alternatives to "the job" as it is narrowly defined and traditionally understood. We should start thinking in terms of a society of alternatives, of hope, not relief and handouts.
I want to turn now to the question of strategy in dealing with the economic prospects that face our country. I want to emphasize certain points which I see as central to our strategy. Dealing first with the phrase "an industrial
Speech from the Throne
strategy," this is a rather glib and popular expression which no one is ready to define with any precision. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) has promised something more definite in his further statements. He contends, and I think rightly, that there has been over the years a developed form of industrial strategy. Programs like PAIT and IRDIA, and policies like the textile policy all constitute a form of industrial strategy. The principal component of the future strategy, and probably the most difficult, will be the steps taken by the department to aid the process of rationalization.
Branch plant fragmentation has demonstrably weakened our domestic economic base. Admittedly the needs of the Canadian consumer have been met, and so have the interests of the U.S. shareholders. But beyond that, the shortcomings of this pattern are clear and have been fully documented by a number of studies. Both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce have referred to this problem and I will await their more precise outline of their plans. I simply want to affirm that in my judgment this has to be a component of our industrial strategy.
Dealing secondly with tax reform, I wish to say that despite the significant and major overhaul of our tax system, it is still apparent that more reforms are necessary. I, for one, am convinced that instead of the extraordinary tax privileges enjoyed by the resource industries to cover their alleged risks, any concessions or privileges available to those industries should be granted on the basis of processing done in Canada. Most resources are in short supply and this situation is likely to continue for some time. It makes no sense to encourage companies to sell our raw materials in basically a sellers' market and give them special subsidies in the process. Tax support, if any in fact is justified, should be geared to support efforts the resource industry makes to process in Canada.
Secondly, consideration will have to be given to tax changes to support venture capital operations in Canada. Even a most cursory examination of the industrial scene will show that a number of small companies with young entrepreneurs and usually some technologically innovative idea, are trying to get off the ground. Their principal problem is trying to find the risk capital necessary. If there are venture capital operations prepared to get into this field, I think the government should share some of the burden. We might examine the methods used in the United States. That could be a formula that would work in Canada; the principle, though, is important and that is that we get into a support position for the venture capital operation. These small businesses funded by venture capital operations often are the kernel out of which much larger, viable and important businesses grow.
Finally, there is national strategy, something I have talked about in this House before. The Minister of Finance, in his speech, expresses the hope that the business community and labour unions, farmers and consumer groups, will make representations and offer advice. This has been, I remind you, Mr. Speaker, to some degree, the pattern of the past. In my view, this process of seeking or offering advice on an ad hoc basis when a situation becomes critical or even the present practice of an annual

February 28, 1972
Speech from the Throne
meeting between the Cabinet and representatives of business and labour-meeting separately, of course-is not adequate to meet the challenges of the present situation. Consultations between labour, management and government have got to be carried on in a far more systematic and continuing basis than heretofore. We have had the good sense to recognize the advantages of continuous consultation in the industrial relations field. The principle applies with equal force on a broader economic front.
Consultations and strategy sessions at the national level will only work if government is prepared to be completely open with the information it has at its disposal. It should also be prepared to consult, in some systematic way, on policy options that are being discussed in Cabinet. I feel very strongly that if labour and business have a clear and continually updated idea of what the government's intentions are, of some of the problems we anticipate, and the leaders of both labour and management are consulted on these matters, we can expect a higher level of co-operation and understanding than has been evinced in our direction heretofore.
Mr. Speaker, I simply say that we face competition in the world from highly developed, sophisticated industrial countries. We face tougher and somewhat protectionist policies from our greatest trading partner and largest market to the south of us. Even all these, and the other problems which I have outlined above, make the closest possible and continuing consultation between government management and labour indispensable. Annual meetings of the kind we have seen in the past will not serve this purpose. They will not produce either the understanding or the co-operation we will need. I appeal to the Minister of Finance, at the start of his new responsibilities, to explore this area of co-operation in a way that, in my view, has not been explored in the past.
I am afraid I am running out of time, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to touch upon an industry which is important in my area, and in relation to which the following statement appeared in the Speech from the Throne:
Policies designed to promote a related, yet distinct, sector of the economy-tourism, will be revealed in coming weeks.
I strongly and enthusiastically endorse this promise, and I will be watching with interest to see what is forthcoming. As you know, Mr. Speaker, representing as I do an area where the tourist industry is very important, I have to say that it faces serious problems in the less developed or advantaged areas. One of the principal problems is that the industry is fragmented and decentralized and does not have the financial base upon which to grow and to rationalize. I think it is important to note the efforts of the IDB in this regard. I point out to the House that last year there was a 56 per cent increase in lending to hotels and motels, from $17 million to $27 million, So, there is movement. It is in the area of financing that the tourist industry, particularly in the less developed areas, requires support.
I would also point out that in less developed areas it is often the tourist industry that holds out the greatest possibility of jobs. Plants are not going to locate in these areas because of the difficulties of transportation and the expense of setting up business, but the tourist industry and the natural resources of the area, lakes, water, hunting and fishing, could provide year round employment.

Any strategy, and this is what I am appealing for, to help less advantaged areas should embrace the following four elements: first, financing on special terms for viable tourist operations whose intention is to grow to meet the sort of criteria we are talking about; second, support for training facilities in our community colleges for people who wish to engage in hotel management or the food service business. Much more sophistication has to be introduced into this area; third, access to tourist areas. Even the most cursory examination of the Kawartha Lakes will demonstrate that access to this area is plagued by inadequate road systems, and most of us are becoming increasingly impatient with the provincial government's performance in support of proper access to the Kawartha area; finally, promotion, particularly within Canada, of possible holidays in other parts. This type of promotion encourages Canadians to move within their country, something that is long overdue.
A coherent, properly financed strategy in this area could do more to meet the inequities faced by the people in the slow growth areas of Ontario and other parts of the country than probably any other strategy. This is something that you, Mr. Speaker, myself and others have been working on for at least two years. I think it is important to take this key phrase from the minister's statement in the House, which reads:

Mr. Speaker, I am sure we all agree that although this move is only a beginning, it marks a radically important victory for those of us who have been saying that these waterways should not be arteries for transportation but should provide the backbone of recreational facilities available to all citizens. What is happening is that the lakes in Ontario and other parts of the country are becoming the closed preserve of a lot of cottage owners. With this program of new priorities there is the possibility that recreation will be available to all citizens, whatever their income and a wide variety of recreational possibilities will be available such as hiking trails, canoe routes, conservation areas, etc. which are a much more exciting prospect than anything held out before.
I strongly commend the minister and the government for making this move. Of all the things that have to be done, the first priority must be to secure land for parks. This is particularly true of the Trent-Severn canal system where land is at a premium and under constant encroachment from private development. If that system is to have land area available to all citizens it is imperative that the federal or the provincial government or the two combined get into a land purchasing program in order to protect it from private development. Of course, private development will continue but in the interests of all a balance must be maintained. The move by this government introduces the hope that such a balance will be estab-

However, I feel compelled to make a couple of observations about the hon. member's verbosity. In the first instance, the Throne Speech itself must have been written by the same team that has been drafting the government's legislation over the past four years. The document was calculated to confuse rather than to enlighten the people of this country and members of this House. It lent itself to as many interpretations as there were listeners and, Mr. Speaker, it failed utterly to provide any solutions to the serious problems which plagued Canada since the present government assumed such extensive powers.
The hon. member for Bruce was like Mark Antony; however, he has something in common with that other Mark Antony. We are not sure whether he came to praise or bury his Caesar. If I may borrow a phrase from the Bard, I think the hon. member protested too much. In the process, he failed to add to the lustre of his Caesar's tarnished image. Apparently he was instructed to deliver his speech in the manner that the government administers its affairs of state, because he rambled and rambled, and in the end was compelled to ask for more time to attempt to make his point. We gladly gave him more time.
I will leave the hon. member for Bruce and turn to the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. McBride). I say to that hon. gentleman that he is much justified in his concern about the probable outcome of the next federal election. When his constituents realize the inconsistencies in the speech he delivered in the House last Monday, his concern will be greatly amplified. In common with my colleagues, I was greatly amazed at the hon. member's statement that he fancies himself as something of an ombudsman. I am anxiously awaiting the day when he will qualify that statement, both by word and deed, and especially by deed.
I should like to make one thing clear before I continue my speech, Mr. Speaker. I am not attacking the two hon. members I have mentioned so far. I am not attacking them personally, anymore than I would launch a personal attack on any member. They are both personal friends of mine. It should be clear to everyone that the subservient backbenchers on the other side of the House relinquished all claims to individuality long ago. They are now reduced to serving the power elite that governs them just as it governs Canada. I am attacking their failure to stand up to the power elite and serve their constituents. I am attacking their subservience and their obvious willingness to put the welfare of their constituents below the welfare of that power elite. The hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton subordinates himself to the will of the elite group which is manipulating this country and then fancies himself an ombudsman. Mr. Speaker, this is a contradiction that, surely, is without equal in the annals of this or any other parliament.
To make my point, may I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that I am not in favour of legislation which would establish an ombudsman in our administrative organization. We are all private members in the House, even the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who represents the riding that elected him; and each of us is the ombudsman for the people he represents.
I am going to answer some of the charges that the hon. member levelled in his speech, some of which deal with the position that some of my colleagues and I have taken against abuses under the Official Languages Act and the Public Service Employment Act. May I say in passing that in my hand I hold a file of complaints of abuses arising under the Public Service Employment Act. That is what I have been pointing out to this House since December 30.
He added that the anguish of civil servants caught up in it is "perfectly legitimate."
"We should be looking to exploit all the mechanisms of the language act to relieve the pressure," he said.
For example, he suggested holders of posts designated as needing bilingual expertise should be given six months' advance notice, to allow them to prepare for it.
The bilingual qualifications for a post also should be suspended for "anybody who has a legitimate claim to a job on the basis of technical competence."
That is the end of the quote from Mr. Spicer, and I thank him for vindicating my stand. The operations of the Public Service Employment Act are a further example of the fuzzy-headedness that has characterized the language policies and all other policies of the present power-oriented government. I serve notice on the government that I shall continue my fight against abuses of the languages act and the corruption of the Public Service Employment Act.
To those who work in the public service and to all of those who aspire to a public service career, I say that I will not abandon them, that I will fight civil service discrimination in the House of Commons and elsewhere, whether it be discrimination against English unilingual-ists or French unilingualists. My reason for that is fundamental, as it was at the beginning of my fight and always will be, namely to see that the youth of Frontenac-Lennox and Addington whom I have the honour to represent in this House have the same opportunity for employment in the public service as those from Levis or Trois-Rivieres.

February 28, 1972
Speech from the Throne

Mr. Speaker, for a few days now, like some other members, I have had a feeling that I am wasting my time listening to the political speeches of the members of the opposition. I have always felt a certain amount of respect for the House of Commons but, since I have come here, I have much less respect for some of the members, who whine and whimper, complain for nothing and about everything, refuse to see the other side of the coin, ridicule, destroy and try to undermine the confidence of the Canadian people in the government and its ability to rule, in spite of failures which, very often, are none of its doing.
Obviously, the members of the opposition are making speeches these days that pertain neither to the Speech from the Throne nor to the routine proceedings in this House, but indeed to the coming election campaign. Yet, their constituents elected them to co-operate with the government when the time comes to pass good legislation such as that contained in the Speech from the Throne. In fact, the opposition has systematically tried to obstruct the passage of many bills since the beginning of the current Parliament. Their constituents will have the right to ask them to give an account of the quality of their so-called obstruction; frankly, I would hate to be in the shoes of a wavering Progressive Conservative, a foiled New Democrat or a swaggering "Caouettiste". I am firmly convinced that Canadians will renew the present government's term of office and strengthen it both as to quality and quantity.
I have had the privilege, Mr. Speaker, of serving for nearly four years now the riding of Madawaska-Victoria. I have served it loyally, honestly and with great dedication. In spite of the distance separating me from my riding, I have still been able to remain in contact with most of my constituents, mainly thanks to the co-operation of the regional weeklies and radio station and also to the indispensable communications tool of modern civilization, the telephone.
Before I go any further, I want to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I can tell the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher), whom we all respect here because of his dedication to the area he represents, I want to say that his continued energy and courage in the face of the repeated but futile attacks of the opposition are two of his major qualities, and we, government members, appreciate him for what he is, a man of integrity, a conscientious and energetic representative of citizens and interests of the riding of Bruce which I had the pleasure of visiting last spring, and of which I have excellent memories.
I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that I am a little less acquainted with the new hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Lajoie). I am, however, aware that he came to us following a by-election, determined to grapple with the problems of his region with the same determination as his lamented predecessor. I wish the hon. member for Trois-Riviere a long political career and great satisfaction in serving his constituents.
I can now speak, Mr. Speaker, of my own riding, of my province, and at the same time of the Atlantic region. I wonder where my riding would be now, without the millions of dollars the government has poured into it over the

past four years. Quite recently, I was still meeting people who asked me to explain why so much money has been allocated to northwestern New Brunswick in recent years.
They are right, Mr. Speaker. For example, and this is far from being a complete account, in the field of education, the federal government has paid to the New Brunswick government $6 million for the construction of composite and trade schools in the Madawaska-Victoria constituency and in the field of culture, the Secretary of State has given to various groups grants amounting to $60,000.
Under the Opportunities for Youth program of 1971, the young people of my area have received $90,000.
Under the Local Initiative Program of 1972, my area has now been awarded by the federal government a total amount of $1,150,000 to create 800 jobs.
Under the regional economic program, many industries have obtained from the department concerned grants totalling over $6 million.
The Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation has granted loans for some $3 million, thus encouraging the construction of low-rent housing and older citizens' dwellings, a thing which had never been done previously.
In agriculture, because of a very desperate situation, especially for potato growers, the federal government twice came to the help of the industry, by paying millions of dollars for price support.
The government has also helped to finance improvements to the regional airport at Edmundston, and the fight against pollution in the St. John River, by spending $3 million. It has provided several millions to improve the educational level of a large number of our fellow-citizens.
I do not want to run through the whole list, Mr. Speaker, and weary hon. members, but, apart from ordinary, administrative and current expenses for the numerous services offered by the Canadian government, the subsidies paid in the last four years have exceeded those of the 25 preceding years to reach a total of approximately $25 million.
I am being told that there is only one Progressive-Conservative member in the House. I do not believe that he is listening to me, that one. But there is nothing new in that.
The people of New Brunswick Mr. Speaker-

I for one have news for the members of the opposition, if they will bother to listen a minute. I shall quote an article which appeared on January 13, 1972 in The Cataract Weekly which, by the way, is a bilingual paper. The heading is as follows:

536 New Jobs Created in Grand Falls [Translation]
This is my native village.

The town of Grand Falls and Victoria County have received as of September 30. 1971 from the Regional Development Incentives Act $3,139,900 which created 536 new jobs in this area. This places Grand Falls second only to Saint John, (the province's largest city) in the creation of new jobs during the past two years. Saint John has obtained the greatest number of new jobs, (1,197), followed by Grand Falls (536), and then by Moncton (311).
This fact was reported in the quarterly publication, "New Brunswick Economic Statistics", issued by the office of the Economic Advisor. The statistics are compiled since the Department of Regional Economic Expansion (DREE) announced its first approvals in October 1969 up to and including September 30,1971.

So, Mr. Speaker, let not the members of the opposition come and try to make us believe that the programs for regional development are not successful. I invite them to visit my area.
Unfortunately, we have heard a lot about bilingualism today, although these questions also concern me enormously since I am bilingual myself and since I represent a bilingual area where the bilingual character of the citizens is respected.
However, I think that I am right in being concerned about the $4 million or so granted by the federal government for the benefit of the schools of the French minority in New Brunswick. I now quote an article published in the paper Le Madawaska on March 31, 1971.
The Societe Nationale des Acadiens is concerned about knowing what will become of the $4 million granted by the federal government for the schools of the official language minority in New Brunswick and for the teaching of second languages.
The association takes advantage of a letter to the New Brunswick Education Minister to question him on that issue and to ask other questions concerning the training of teachers in the field of vocational education, the absence of Francophones in the vocational education division of the New Brunswick Education Department, the almost complete absence of French-speaking specialists in the curriculum and research division and what will become of the pupils attending the bilingual school in Fredericton now that the Health Department has condemned it.
I am glad to say that the matter of the bilingual school at Fredericton has been settled. A decent building has been provided for the young students and I congratulate the population of Fredericton for making that decision.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government granted $4 million to the province of New Brunswick, and I have learned from a reliable source, within the last few days, that those $4 million had been allocated to the General Income Fund of that province, so that absolutely nothing is done to promote bilingualism, certaindy not to the advantage of the New Brunswick minority. During the last few days, I got in touch with the
Speech from the Throne
Secretary of State and I asked for a report on that unfortunate situation.
The funny thing about all this is that the government which has to administer those $4 million is a conservative government which came to power in October 1969. And I quote now an article from a first-rate newspaper, Le Madawaska-

The shameful thing, Mr. Speaker, is that the Conservatives who themselves wrote that resolution are now in power in New Brunswick and have done nothing to promote bilingualism. On the contrary, the population was able to realize the lamentable state of bilingualism following the film "L'Acadie" and the regrettable incidents which took place in Moncton.
How can you explain the lack of confidence of the French-speaking population of New Brunswick in the present government? How can you explain all the events which are taking place on the eastern and northern shores of New Brunswick? Can you blame those people for establishing their own political party, the Parti acadien? I would be ashamed to be a Progressive Conservative today! I would be ashamed to be in power in New Brunswick and be unable to serve the interests of the two founding groups of this country equitably, in a province which officially calls itself bilingual.
Fortunately, while receding in many areas, we have also made some progress.
