-had little to offer the people of Canada when it came to power but the slogan "the just society". It had no policies for the latter part of the sixties but rode in on the economic and financial momentum generated in the early part of the decade. As we move into the decade of the seventies and are faced with mounting economic problems reflecting the growing complexity of national and international relations, and so on, it is disappointing to find a Speech from the Throne which has no policies for this important decade.
In an election year it would seem to me that the government would have something to offer more than style to the people of Canada. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) moves about the hustings, testing the atmosphere and mood of the nation, I notice that he does not -quite know whether to go for broke with elaborate promises or attempt to repeat the tour de force of 1968 when he was able to get by without promising anything, creating the impression that his was a new style, a new era, the dawn of the age of Aquarius.
Mr. Speaker, the amendment placed before Parliament by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) is right on target and I trust it will have support from all members of the House. The amendment would add the following words to the motion:
but we find intolerable the utter failure of this government to bring forward a decisive policy to achieve full employment and
Speech from the Throne
the continuing uncertainty and hesitancy in the economy because of the chronic indecisiveness of this government.
I am sure that when we use the phrase "we find intolerable," we are speaking for the people of Canada. But I shall deal with that later in my remarks.
It is true that economic issues are the mainspring of any government policy. As the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Peddle) said in his speech this afternoon, the B and B issues are fundamental-the "bread and butter" issues. As I move around the Canadian body politic, I realize this is where the buck is lying at the present time. There are the issues of great concern to the majority of the people of Canada.
When we say in the motion that the government is indecisive and lacks a sense of leadership, it is because the record of the past four years has indicated that the government's approach to economic problems is an ad hoc, unplanned approach. This ad hoc, unplanned approach reflects the personality of the Prime Minister who, after all, is the leader of this House and the leader of the government.
His whole life style and his excursion into politics has been that of an individual uncertain of his personal commitment in terms of party, in terms of policy and in terms of program as he now exercises the supreme responsibility of leader of this nation. He came to this House in 1965, recently converted from the New Democratic Party. He is not the only one in the present Cabinet to have that pedigree. There should be a fundamental difference between the philosophy of the NDP and that of the Liberal party which he presently supports. If there is not, I am sure that explains why there is lack of dynamic and sure-footed leadership at this time.

Some of the main initiatives of the present government, Mr. Speaker, have reflected this unplanned, ad hoc approach to the major issues before us. We are a northern nation beset every year by winter unemployment. This applies in western Canada, particularly the prairie west, perhaps more than in the other areas because of the severity of winter conditions there.
I well remember the Prime Minister indicating that he was no longer going to use the excellent winter works program that had been developed by the Conservative administration which occupied the treasury benches between 1957 and 1963 because there was not going to be any fundamental problem of unemployment. So the "Do it now, why wait for spring?" program was set aside. In its place, for the last two years, because of the chronic problem of unemployment we have had the ad hoc Local Initiatives Program, the Opportunites for Youth program, and so forth, instead of deliberate planning to meet a severe problem.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House recessed at six o'clock I was pointing out to hon. members that the basic criticism we direct at the present government led by the Prime Minister is that it has failed to deal realistically with economic and financial matters. Instead of being presented with a co-ordinated, national economic policy in which the priorities would have been set by the people and the people's representatives, we have been led through an incomprehensible maze plotted by this super group surrounding the Prime Minister's office and involved in all the activities of the government generally. The result is, Mr. Speaker, that the private sector of the economy has been stifled because of the smothering effect of the super group.
I recall the words of a distinguished Senator who put on record in the other place precisely what has happened. I read from a report in the Globe and Mail written under the heading, "Liberal Senator attacks policies of government":
Senator Daniel Lang, . . . Toronto lawyer and business executive, charged that the Trudeau government is alienating businessmen by its tax legislation, its proposed changes in competition and labour laws and its promotion of friendship with the Soviet Union.
He argued that the future of Canadian confederation itself depends on good relations between business and government and called for a rapid return to that condition of mutual respect-'
Senator Lang, former treasurer and campaign chairman for the Liberal party in Ontario, was speaking in a Senate debate on the Canadian economy.
He raised issues that have been the subject of growing complaints by businessmen lately.
He said private business was uncertain and fearful of administrative powers given to the public service.
I am afraid that many in the private sector regard this bureaucracy as aloof, intransigent, doctrinaire and oftimes hostile,' he said.
It is obvious that some hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches have become concerned by the present economic course of the administration. I was interested in a speech that crossed my desk not long ago. It was delivered to the Canadian Club in the Hotel Vancouver on Friday February 4, by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), who is the hon. member for Capilano, if I may refer to him by naming his constituency. The title of the speech was, "Canada's economic Oscar".
According to the speech, which continued for 21 pages, the Minister of the Environment was obviously more concerned about the political environment than about the physical environment, because he was at great pains to point out that all was for the best in the best of all possible worlds. I read from page 18 of that speech the following remarks:
I know you're worried about our new Competition Act. But this legislation is being withdrawn. It's being rewritten. The emphasis is being put, increasingly, on competition. I'm sure that you agree, at least in principle, that competition is a good thing. More competition rather than less will be a good thing for Canada just as it has been a good thing elsewhere-
Confidence and competition; the two go hand in hand. I personally believe in an open economy. I believe, wholeheartedly, in individual initiative. I believe in private enterprise. I believe, also, that Canadians can be enterprising.

I agree that Canadians can be enterprising if they are given a chance and not smothered under the overwhelming influence of the present bureaucratic structure of government particularly in the office of the Prime Minister. I have a recent comment on the attitude of business toward government policy as reported in the Globe and Mail "Report on business" of February 23. Hon. members can read this report for themselves. The article is headlined, "Economic Council predicts slowdown in capital spending", and I quote:
The veil of gloom that permeated business circles last October, and has only recently been partly lifted, has yielded the most pessimistic forecast of capital spending plans ever made by the 1 Economic Council of Canada.
The president of DuPont found fault with industrial and tariff policies. I quote the following excerpt of his words:
Current government policy is for an open economy and industry that is world-competitive. But this is not consistent with a proposed new Competition Act that would fragment industry, with regional-development policies that have philosophical merit but are economically disastrous, with a technical innovation system that is different from and more restrictive than those of other areas.
The former minister of consumer and corporate affairs is a neighbour of the hon. member for Capilano, the Minister of the Environment. I am sure that the transition in ministerial responsibility is further proof of the growing disease that exists among the business community and the Canadian body politic. It is not only in big business; it also affects small business, farmers and wage earners. We were recently in our constituencies for a particularly long recess. If hon. members will speak the truth on the matter,
I am sure they will admit they were beset and besieged by farmers, businessmen and indeed all Canadians with regard to the uncertainties arising from the impact of the so-called tax reform measure that was forced through the House under closure just before the Christmas recess.
Last week a member of the House, a former deputy prime minister, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), summed it up in these words, "The government's economic policies are stupid and even subversive." That sums up the situation as seen by someone who obviously had inside information as a key member of the Trudeau administration.
I want to speak briefly on a matter that I know something about personally, and refer to comments made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) in his speech in the House on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. He gave forth, under the title "The quality of Canadian life":
We want to safeguard those diversities, to give them full play in the shaping of a proud Canadianism which reflects all the elements of our society.
The hon. gentleman was reading from a printed text that was distributed to the press and members of the House concerning in general terms the quality of Canadian life. He was not necessarily dealing with economic matters. I want to give the hon. gentleman credit; since he assumed his portfolio he has grown in stature in office. From the quotation I have just read to hon. members, obviously he has gained wide understanding of the new dimensions in Canadian confederation.
February 28, 1972

I shall not go into detail on some of the economic matters he dealt with in connection with northern affairs, because we welcome him to the family circle of those who in the past decade or more have regarded the great undeveloped part of northern Canada in the Yukon and Northwest Territories as the last great frontier of Canadian development. News of oil discoveries, news of a boom in mineral development and national parks in the north were subjects being discussed and planned when the vision of northern development was regarded with scepticism by members on the opposite side of the House. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has now become the chief exponent of this enthusiasm.
I want to link the quotation with regard to the proud Canadianism which reflects all elements of society to another major responsibility of the hon. gentleman; that is, developing policies and programs for our native Canadians. The real resources of Canada are human resources. The area of development of human resources, particularly our native population in the territories as well as in other parts of Canada, is where the government has been sadly negligent. If we are to achieve a quality of Canadian life adequate for our first Canadians, be they Indians, Eskimos or Metis, we must recognize the basic rights of all elements of Canadian society. In particular, we must recognize land claims and aboriginal rights which thus far have been short-circuited by this administration.
When the Prime Minister was specifically confronted with these matters he told these people, who are an important element of the great Canadian mosaic, to forget their traditions and become good Canadians. I suppose the proper response to that statement by the Prime Minister would be, "Physician, heal thyself."
It is true that human resources is the main ingredient in the development of this nation. In the few moments that remain at my disposal I wish to point out that this is another area of serious neglect on the part of the administration, particularly as it applies to western Canada. It has been said that mankind is one, the human family is one, but cultures are many. There is a new dimension of Canadianism that has emerged outside of upper and lower Canada, that has not yet been fully grasped by this administration. There is no dominant cultural group in western Canada. The compact theory of Confederation does not necessarily apply there, nor is it readily accepted. Rather, we are faced with a mosaic which is as colourful as the Canadian maple leaf.
Western Canada is not willing to become lumped material to be shaped in the image of the Prime Minister of Canada. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) used a word which is loaded with emotion-several other hon. members have mentioned it-in describing the Premier of a western province as a bigot, he was not contributing much to the dialogue respecting national unity. The premier of British Columbia was pointing out that if bilingual qualifications were to become a major requirement among those seeking job opportunities in the capital of the nation, then people from western Canada would clearly be discriminated against. This point was raised repeat-
Speech from the Throne
edly by spokesmen from western Canada during the debate on the official languages issue.
The situation, has of course, been aggravated by other measures taken by the government such as the changing of names which are an integral part of the heritage of western Canada. It is easy for the Prime Minister to make a joke about changing the historical and traditional description of what used to be the Northwest Mounted Police, and later became the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to the simple word "police", but it is not being accepted in western Canada. I was in the west last week and I am aware of the strong feeling on this issue in all the western provinces. I am sure the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) is aware of it too.
The time has come, it seems, for two provinces in Canada, or one province for that matter, to refrain from imposing its image on the rest of Canada. A multicultural society is emerging which expresses the real spirit of Canadianism in this second half of the twentieth century. The Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) will be in Vancouver within the next couple of weeks. Obviously, he recognizes this problem because he will be participating in an important conference promoted by the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews concerning the implications of the policy of multiculturalism in this country. I say again that the situation is not being resolved when the Queen's first minister describes the Premier of one of the western provinces, in the course of a public statement, as a bigot. In other words, if you do not agree with the Prime Minister you are a bigot. It is an expletive which will not be accepted in the west.
There are two further matters I should like to bring to the attention of the House, if I have time. They concern government efficiency. If you have no policies which are going anywhere in terms of economic development, I suppose it is impossible for there to be administrative efficiency. We are faced with a breakdown of administrative efficiency at the senior level of government. I refer, of course, to the unemployment insurance fiasco which has been causing severe headaches to all members of the House of Commons, the immigration situation, the strikes which have been dislocating the public service in the past few weeks, and particularly the strike which has been tying up Canada's air service to such a degree that it is bound to have a profound adverse effect on the economic well-being of the nation.
I refer also to discontent which has been rampant among the staff of the Post Office. As critic for the official opposition in this field, I have spent much of my time receiving and replying to complaints in this area. People are seeking improvement in the quality of the basic service which is supposed to be provided by the Post Office Department, and I do not think that the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) or the government as a whole pay the slightest attention to these complaints. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read one or two of these complaints into the record.

To reply briefly, I have been overwhelmed by complaints from my constituency concerning the closing of rural post offices, as the hon. member knows. But in this debate I am trying not to be parochial; I am trying to show that the problem is one of national, even international significance. The following letter was written by a lady doctor in Denver, Colorado. Strong language is used, which I shall not put on the record. She writes:
Since October 21, 1971, no communication written by me has ever been received in St. Catharines. In addition to this, since that date, none of the communications from St. Catharines has been received by me .. . Would you please send someone to find where all of those sacks of mail have been for all of these months and could you please get them delivered? I would be eternally grateful.
That letter, too, was directed to the Prime Minister, among others. I could read many more, similar complaints but my time has expired. I shall conclude by saying that in 1963 the Prime Minister wrote of the Liberal government of that day:
There is not one man in this party to whom principles mean more than power.
The same men, the men of whom he wrote so bitterly, sit beside him on the government front benches today. Nothing has changed except the title of the jobs they hold, and their grim determination to hang on to office at any cost is as evident today as it was ten years ago.
I would urge hon. gentlemen opposite, if they really want to understand what is going on in Canada, to get out and listen to the people. The old slogan, "Power, patronage and perpetuity", which has long been a slogan adhered to by successive Liberal governments, will not be realized following the next election.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join my colleagues in this House in congratulating the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne for a job well done.
I am rising today to speak about the government's plans to improve the fabric of Canadian social justice. I hope to back up these plans by establishing the bona fides of the government in this area over the past few months, and certainly during its term of office. In doing so, I bear in mind what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) stated in his address to the House last week. He said that statistics are no substitute for the individual citizen's well-being. We can talk all we like about participatory democracy, we can mention the millions of dollars that we have spent or intend to spend on items like old age security, family income security, medicare, hospital insurance, rehabilitative welfare services and the like, but in the end a satisfactory participation level depends upon the individual.
When we talk about the individual in the context of social justice, we come down to the individual's alienation from the society in which he lives and from his fellow Canadians, all of whom contribute to the cause of this feeling of alienation. We are familiar with many of these causes: the bigness of our institutions-the "bigness" syndrome of industrially-developed countries like Canada. This tends to make the individual feel small, to make him feel that his role is sometimes meaningless and lost.
All this has resulted from rapid technological change and great innovations in the area of automation and cybernation. This alienation is also contributed to by the rising expectations which our consumer-oriented society all too often is geared to create but unable to fulfil. Once these rising expectations are created, individuals feel alienated by poverty, by feeling uncertain in an era of rapid social change. They are fearful because the old values on which they base their pattern of life and look to for certain security for the future no longer seem to be there.
February 28, 1972

Therefore, when we talk about alienation of the individual and the participation level of the individual in society, we must concern ourselves with policies designed to cope with the situation. The three components of this policy seem to me, depending of course on the nature and quality of the service to the individual, to break down, firstly, to that of economic security, secondly, access to services and, thirdly, the individual's involvement in decision-making.
First let me talk about the individual's economic security as a way of combating his alienation from society and his fellow man. By "economic security" we are really talking about finding jobs for the individual. To a large extent this is what economic security means to him.
What has the government done to establish its bona fides in regard to future plans? May I talk about those who are already employed-the employables, if you like. I am talking not only of those who are employed but of those who are employable and are waiting to get into the labour force. What are some of the government's policies for them? Under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce we have the PAIT program which is designed to encourage industry to make breakthroughs in areas of new technology: we award them grants to carry on and develop that new technology. That is one example. Export development grants is another program of the government. Accelerated rates of depreciation is another. Setting up boards, such as the textile review board, to encourage industry in their particular area and to keep that sector of our industry alive is yet another policy of the government.
The second area of stimulation of the private sector in terms of job creation is the attention we have paid to slow-growth areas through our regional development programs. Thirdly in the area of providing stimulation to the private sector to provide jobs, I think we should mention our manpower training program and our encouragement to industry to provide training within industry itself through direct government grants. In this connection I refer also to direct grants under the Local Initiatives Program and the winter employment municipal loans fund. It seems to me that all these programs are designed to encourage the private sector to provide jobs.
There is also the Opportunities for Youth program. In terms of our youth, this program is designed to encourage the private sector to provide jobs for youth. These are some of the many policies that have been implemented by this government over recent months and years to provide a degree of economic security for Canadians.
As I mentioned at the beginning, these policies were designed for those Canadians who are employable. Within that category, of course, there are Canadians who are employable but who have special problems which for one reason or another are inhibitors in terms of their finding ready access to the labour market. There are three areas here about which I wish to speak. Firstly, there are the physically handicapped. What have we done for these people? We have the vocational rehabilitation program, and we have very recently increased veterans disability pensions.
Secondly, we have the socially and emotionally handicapped, those who unfortunately have a minimum of
Speech from the Throne
education, who are often below manpower retraining standards and have suffered from long-term unemployment. What are some of our policies to help these people? We have the work activity projects under the Canada Assistance Plan which are covered by a cost-sharing arrangement with the provinces. Lately we have very much encouraged the provinces to take greater advantage of this provision under the Canada Assistance Plan and to submit work activity projects that carry with them personal counselling and professional help to the long-term unemployed in order to help them acquire work habits which would enable them to re-enter the labour market.
Another group of employables who have special problems is mothers who are alone, or spouses without partners who have children they must support and who are considered employable. It would enrich their lives as well as their children's lives if they could enter the labour market. What have we done in this area? Under the Canada Assistance Plan we provide financial assistance, under a cost-sharing arrangement with the provinces, to provide day-care centres. In the fiscal year 1971-72 the federal government spent approximately $4 million for this purpose which, counting the provincial share, represents over $8 million in the last fiscal year to commence, in combination with the private sector, a network of daycare centres to allow mothers who are alone to go into the labour market to pick up either full-time or part-time work.
Also, in discussing the provision of economic security for individuals we must also take into account those people in our work force who are unemployable, who are permanently out of the work force and who could not re-enter it even if they wanted to do so. What have we done for this group of people? Of course, a very large segment of the Canadian population which is permanently out of the work force is our senior citizens, many of whom, because of infirmity or advanced age, could not work even if they were desirous of doing so and even if the government wished them to do so.
Recently we raised the level of the guaranteed income supplement. No matter what criticism it may be subject to, the government has raised the basic income floor for over one million Canadians who now obtain the guaranteed income supplement either in whole or in part to levels which are now nearly approaching the level of adequacy and which are far more generous than anything we have known before.
I spoke about policies designed to help senior citizens who are permanently out of the work force. The next group of individuals with whom we must concern ourselves, who are permanently out of the work force, is the disabled. As indicated in the white paper on income security, the government has shown that this is a group of people we must next take into consideration. The white paper spoke about applying the same technique as is applied in the guaranteed income supplement to the disabled, so as to provide them with a basic guaranteed minimum income upon which they can rely. It can be subject to an income test and does not carry with it the humiliation of a means or a needs test.
We spoke about what we have done for the employables in terms of stimulating the private sector; we spoke about employables with special problems and about some of the

February 28, 1972
Speech from the Throne
programs we have devised to assist these people. We spoke about the unemployed who are permanently out of the work force. There is another group of Canadians who are suffering from low incomes, that is people who are in the work force but who are earning marginal incomes. What has the government done for them, and what does it plan to do to assist them?
In terms of the federal government's capacity to do so, and in terms of our jurisdiction under the constitution, we have provided increases in the minimum wage levels for all working in industries falling within federal jurisdiction, during the life of this Parliament, to the degree that those levels are well in advance of most of the minimum wage laws of the provinces. I do not say this with any degree of exultation, but I think all hon. members are aware of it.
What else have we done for many Canadians in the work force earning marginal incomes? Many of them are veterans for whom we have provided increases during the life of this Parliament under war veterans allowances. This does provide income supplementation for them. I would refer in this regard to the recent tax bill of the former minister of finance, which provided assistance to people earning marginal incomes whereby upward of one million persons were taken off the tax rolls entirely.
I might speak here about all the people who fall in this category and who have benefited from the greatly enriched benefit structure of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Of course, I should refer also to a policy we have discussed in this Parliament, one on which I have spoken, on behalf of the government, with the provinces. I refer to the Family Income Security Plan which I hope to bring before this House very soon. This will afford meaningful income supplementation to hundreds of thousands of families the heads of which are in the labour force and are working but are working at marginal incomes.
This plan provides for that inevitable deficiency which occurs in the private sector where private industry rewards a man on the basis of his ability and his value to that particular industry, but without any regard to his dependants. The Family Income Security Plan takes this increased dependency into account and provides income supplementation.
I have spoken of some of the policies already adopted and some we intend to adopt in terms of assistance to that group of individuals who are already in the work force but are earning too little in many cases. Now I would like to move on to the second major area which I identified in my opening remarks in terms of a basic policy designed to cope with the alienation of the individual and to enhance social justice in Canada, that is, access to services.
This area is very important indeed but is one about which we do not talk very much in Parliament. We all know that the health of the individual is basic to his person and to his family. In the area of personal health, we know that Canada, in relation to many of the countries in the free world, has one of the lowest ratios of doctors to population and one of the lowest ratios of hospital beds to population. At the same time, we know that in relative terms we have a well developed health delivery system. But we know there are deficiencies in terms of the distribution of these services, in terms of the distribution

throughout Canada of our doctors, of our medical health and health personnel and especially in terms of lack of adequate distribution in low-income areas and in rural areas.
What has the government endeavoured to do in this area? We have suggested a new policy to the provinces, the new health cost-sharing arrangements. They are designed to keep costs to a reasonable level. This is essential if we are not to price these services beyond the public's ability to pay and perhaps risk total public disapproval of schemes such as medicare and hospitalization, which I think a majority of the members of this House endorse.
What else have these policies been designed to do? They have been designed to sponsor new health delivery systems in order to bring them closer to the public. I have talked about the new cost-sharing formula and in particular the Thrust fund provision that will give greater flexibility to the provinces to develop community health centres and services which will relieve the burden on active treatment facilities that are so costly, and in many cases are utilized by people who do not really need them. Among other things that the policies are designed to do is bring about improved redistribution of resources. Here I refer to the special incentives to doctors to move into rural areas and thus improve our distribution of health personnel.
The Thrust fund will also help provinces to undertake new schemes in this area. It will allow them to develop new paramedical personnel, which will relieve the burdensome task on many of our doctors who are now providing a service that, because of their high qualifications, in effect is a waste. Many doctors admit that all too many of their man-hours are spent on tasks which other trained personnel could perform just as adequately.
Of course, one of the basic fundamental philosophies in the whole health cost proposals is the great emphasis we are placing on preventive techniques, which will mean greater improvement in health services for Canadians. In recent years we have put too much emphasis on curative medicine as distinct from preventive medicine. The Thrust fund and the new health cost-sharing proposals will also encourage such programs as mass screening that will detect illnesses which have not yet come to the surface, thus allowing a quicker response to them and allowing us to save many lives that might otherwise be lost. Here I am talking about mass immunization programs and much greater emphasis on public health programs, including improvement of the diet of all Canadians.
In talking about access to services, I might also mention what we have also done in the health area but we often do not think of in terms of health programs, but which nevertheless forms part of them. I am talking about the program to enhance the physical fitness of Canadians. Here I would refer briefly to the creation of Sport Canada and Recreation Canada. Over the course of the last three years the financial resources put into these areas have been more than doubled.
Dealing with this subject, I refer to the agency specifically set up to increase participation in physical recreation which enjoys the co-operation of both government and industry and which can call on the private sector,
February 28, 1972

especially the media, that is, television, newspapers and radio, to combine with us in packaging programs which can have a much greater impact upon Canadians. Here, in terms of past bona fides, I talk of our Cross-Canada Sports Demonstration, and our Sports Caravan which is now going around many parts of this country, bringing the message of physical fitness and sports involvement directly to the mass of the public and schoolchildren.
I also talk about government programs designed to increase local facilities through grants under DREE, and the winter employment municipal grants. I also refer to our department's facility survey conducted last summer- will be conducted again this coming summer-to help rural areas develop greater use of facilities already in existence. Of course, I also refer to the Opportunities for Youth program and the Local Initiatives Program which have assisted work in the recreational area, with people at the grass-roots level. I also refer to grants to groups such as Indian bodies to permit them to develop recreational and physical fitness programs.
Here, too, I talk about our sports administration centre which has brought together on a more adequate basis the administrative people in our sports bodies, thus assisting them in the technical area in terms of coaching so that they in turn can stimulate greater use of facilities in Canada and a greater degree of mass participation in sports. I also refer to our Canadian Games which now are almost a national event in Canada, in addition to the Canadian Olympics. Under both programs we give grants to municipalities to develop sports and recreational facilities for the long term.
I refer also the Canadian fitness awards scheme which we have introduced to all primary and secondary schools in Canada, which is designed to provide incentive to our young people to acquire awards in accordance with the standards set out in the scheme. I also refer to our scholarship program which is encouraging many of our young people to be an example to the rest of the Canadian public. These are some of the positive programs we are undertaking in this area on the health side.
But, Mr. Speaker, some negative influences have been at work in our community on the health side, of which hon. members are aware. Here I refer to the misuse of drugs by an all too alarming number of Canadians. In this area we have commissioned the LeDain report. That commission has already brought in a preliminary report, and more recently the first instalment of its final report on treatment. I would point out that we had acted on many of the recommendations even before the final report on treatment came out. Here I refer in particular to our recent action which received the general approbation of hon. members, placing greater restrictive use on amphetamines and methadone.
Under our drug abuse program we have taken steps to get into the area of street-level analysis and into the area of research into illicit drugs. There are also the innovative service grants that we established during the last two years which give grants to local agencies to help people with drug problems as well as related problems connected with food, clothing and shelter, and diseases that all too often go with drug abuse, such as VD. We have funded drop-in centres and crisis centres to help people who are
Speech from the Throne
having so-called bad trips or are suffering very serious illness because of drug abuse.
I also refer to funds provided for public education programs designed to establish a basis of credibility so that we can motivate Canadians, especially young people who have not yet resorted to drugs, not to do so and to persuade those committing drug abuse to discontinue their habit.
Another area, in terms of access to services, is that of the impact of the law on the individual. In the Speech from the Throne we heard of the intention of the Minister of Justice to provide a legal aid, in combination with the provinces, to those who have been charged with criminal offences.
I think the House may be well aware of what we have done on the civil side, and particularly at the lower income level, through our national welfare grants. Here we have been prepared to fund at the local level organizations which are prepared to emphasize, first the curative side and then the preventive side in terms of legal services. On the curative side I refer, in terms of assistance, to people who have, for example, landlord and tenant problems or debtor and creditor problems. On the preventive side, with the aid of our grants people can receive counselling on their rights, especially in the consumer area in which many low-income people suffer discrimination. With respect to welfare appeal rights, our grants can assist them to better learn what their rights are.
I would refer to the advocative side where we would talk in terms of funding some groups to bring group action in pollution cases, urban redevelopment cases and tenants' rights organizations; this would allow them to better organize in order to present their point of view. There are techniques here, such as those the government has, which can be used to assist individuals to have access to services.
On the legislative side there is, of course, a role for government, Mr. Speaker, both before and after any confrontation with the law which may be necessary. First, I should like to deal with the preventative side where legislation is designed to assist the individual before any involvement with the courts and the adversary system. There are the government programs for consumer protection. One which I am sure stands out in our minds was brought into this House by the previous minister of consumer and corporate affairs and was passed. This was part X of the Bankruptcy Act, where a person in the low-income category, a debtor, can now have greater access to public trustees to advance a declaration of his bankruptcy in order to become devoid of his debts. Another is the Bills of Exchange Act. At one time, upon a third party assumption of a promissory note, the third party did not have to accept any of the obligations of the person with whom the debtor originally made the contract. This situation has been corrected.
Legislation has been implemented on the rehabilitation side. I refer to the Criminal Code amendments announced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) a few days ago. The highlights are conditional and absolute discharge, intermittent sentences and matters that the Solicitor General

February 28, 1972
Speech from the Throne
(Mr. Goyer) and the Minister of Justice have talked about in terms of penal reform.
Having talked about the individual in terms of our health legislation and policies and in relation to our law, I should now like to speak about families and how we have assisted them in terms of access to services. One area is housing. I would point out that in 1971 we had the highest record in dwelling houses built in Canada, with a record number of homes for low-income families. In the Speech from the Throne the government has referred to fresh new concepts in neighbourhood improvement and new emphasis on low-cost housing.
I refer, as well, to our policies in the Department of National Health and Welfare relative to family planning where this information is made available to everybody. Too often only the higher income groups have had access to this information, but our program is designed to provide it to all regardless of income.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members. I think I can finish in five minutes. I should like to mention some of the policies of the government which have general application in terms of access to services. There are the initiatives we have taken in regard to nutritional upgrading. I have written to many hon. members about the Nutrition Canada survey which is going on now and which will permit us to ascertain the diets of Canadians, their eating habits, so that we can design policies to improve or correct these. The findings of this survey will be available soon.
I have spoken of improved health services for our native peoples. In the last three years we have increased the budget to the point where the native people themselves are prepared to admit that the program has improved. I think it is safe to predict that the infant mortality rate amongst our native peoples will decrease. I have spoken also about the action taken to reduce the high cost of prescription drugs. We have enclosed with the old age pension cheques and family allowance cheques a list of the comparative prices of drugs. A quality inspection system has been established within the Food and Drug Directorate, and in the course of the next year and a half we will be able to send information to physicians showing them that on the basis of our tests they can depend, where it is so, on generic drugs and brand name drugs being of equal quality.
Many physicians have indicated that they are not prepared to prescribe a generic drug because they are not confident that its quality is equivalent to the brand name drug. We are prepared to increase funding in order to give them that assurance. This program will bring down the cost of drugs. I refer, also, to action taken in this area by the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs in 
terms of the Patent Act which has had the effect of bringing down the cost of drugs.
Mr. Speaker, I have talked about two main areas, the economic security proposals of the government and access to services. We have brought in meaningful prroposals designed to combat poverty and to increase the participation level of the individual and thus bring about a greater degree of social justice. The third area, one in which I cannot enlarge to any degree due to time constraint, is access to decision-making. I would point out the many programs we have designed such as the Opportunities for Youth program, innovative service grants in the drug abuse area and welfare grants to enable low-income people to organize and express their views. Then there are the minority group citizenship grants under the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), which allow people to organize and present their views and preserve their very distinct qualities as Canadians, and the multicultural grants recently announced by the Secretary of State. All these are designed to enhance the accessibility of the decision-making process to Canadians.
We have used as a government the participation role in the design of policies. This technique was used in the white paper on tax reform and I have used it in my department on income security programs where we have received input from people knowledgeable in that field. There is our recent action in terms of providing greater equality to women. We have received the royal commission report and many departments, including my own, are providing a greater role for women who are being appointed to more national boards and, within my department, to advisory boards where they have equality in designing social policies. There are also policies designed to involve our retired citizens. I refer of course, to the Canadian Executive Service Overseas program under the Department of External Affairs. Also under our welfare grants programs we are providing funds to enable senior citizens to come together in meaningful endeavours.
In conclusion, from the Speech from the Throne we learn that we can look forward to new policies in terms of access to services, such as new policies in housing, new policies in terms of more humane treatment of offenders and in the area of drugs. In terms of economic security we can expect policies in the family income security area and policies designed to provide compensation for victims of crime. There is a rich record of governmental accomplishment in terms of social justice in these three main areas. These are three main, necessary areas involving social justice for Canadians. Certainly, the proposals in the Speech from the Throne will enhance these policies and bring social justice, as a reality, closer to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I was most interested to hear the minister's speech. There is no doubt that his department and other departments of government have brought forward many programs over the past four years. I was interested to hear him say that to a great extent one of our big problems today is that of human alienation. It would be funny, if it were not so tragic, to suggest that despite the hundreds of millions of dollars being spent today by this government, in my opinion people today are more isolated than ever before. They feel
February 28, 1972

more alienated than ever before from a computer-oriented, de-personalized government. It makes little difference if you talk about new programs in terms of quantity: it is quality and closeness to the individual in society that counts, so far as I am concerned.

Mr. Speaker, even though it is not the first speech I have made in the House, I should like to take this opportunity to tell hon. members something about my constituency. This will not be the usual, flowery description of the greatest little corner of Canada, for surely this is too serious an occasion for that; but it will be, rather, an analysis of many of the ill effects the present regime has had on that constituency.
One of the main reasons, Mr. Speaker, why many people in Brant did not vote for the Liberal candidate in the by-election last spring was that they had become disillusioned with Liberal party policies. Today, if you go west, that disillusionment is even greater. If you go east, the disillusionment is greater, too. This government is a government whose major strength came from central Canada in 1968-and my riding, Brant, is in central Canada. So the disillusionment today is not only widespread but intensive in central Canada, where the party in power had its strength four years ago.
As far as population is concerned, Mr. Speaker, the federal riding of Brant consists mainly of the city of Brantford, the town of Paris and the villages of Burford and St. George, with a combined population of some
75,000	people. Rural Brant is populated mainly by good, progressive farmers specializing in dairying, beef, hogs and cash cropping. Both urban and rural Brant have suffered as a result of government policies-or lack of them.
To begin, I should like to discuss the single, most pressing problem in urban, and to some extent rural, Brant. I am, of course, referring to unemployment. Since 1970 the official rate of unemployment has hovered around the 8 per cent mark. The unofficial rate has gone to between 12 and 15 per cent, thanks to the former minister of finance's bungling of the economy. His name has become a pretty miserable household word in my riding. The unofficial rate of between 12 and 15 per cent was given to me by an employee of the Unemployment Insurance Commission in Hamilton.
The present government has become famous for its almost zealous devotion to statistics. But, Mr. Speaker, let us look at the flesh and blood behind the statistics. Let us look at the misery and social dislocation caused by severe unemployment in just one riding, where unemployment insurance claimants are being forced to go on the welfare rolls because of the ineptitude and utter chaos that now reigns in the Unemployment Insurance Commission throughout this country. I receive 25 to 30 phone calls a day and 20 letters a week. The vast majority of these cases concern unemployment and unemployment insurance.
Mr. Speaker, I was elected to represent all the interests of Brant. I was elected to be a parliamentarian. Considering the salary I receive, I do not think that 75 per cent of my time should be devoted to acting as a troubleshooter for the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
Speech from the Throne

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Since I was elected I have never shunned my responsibility as a member whose primary concern has always been the best interests of his riding. People, out of desperation, phone me to see if I can get them a job or an unemployment insurance cheque. Contrary to popular opinion, the vast majority of unemployed persons in my riding and elsewhere in Canada in fact wants to work. For a man to sit around home all day is both degrading and depressing. He loses his sense of worth as head of a family and eventually begins to lose his self-respect. Yet our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who has never had to go through the agony of hustling for a job in his life, has the unmitigated gall to tell the jobless of this country, most of whom are out of work as a direct result of his stupid and irrational economic policies, that there are all kinds of jobs across the country if only the unemployed would get up off their behinds and go to where the jobs are.
The Prime Minister reminds me of some of the Paraohs of ancient Egypt summoning the masses to come and chip stone and build a pyramid. He also says, outside the House, in his heartless way that the jobless will not work because they will not accept a wage of $1.75 an hour. Who can raise a family today with dignity and hope, in this "just society", on $1.75 an hour?
What the Prime Minister has failed to tell the jobless is that there are approximately 40,000 jobs chasing nearly
700,000	unemployed, and that most of those 40,000 job vacancies require highly skilled persons, not the kind presently going through manpower retraining. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, manpower retraining has become just another Liberal gimmick to reduce unemployment figures. Most of the trainees, who have been trained at tremendous expense to the taxpayer, find it virtually impossible to obtain gainful employment after finishing their courses. In fact, Mr. Speaker, there is virtually no relationship between manpower retraining courses and present job vacancies. I think this illustrates once again the almost total lack of economic planning on the part of the mod-squad government with which this country is presently faced.
As for moving around the country in search of work, I am reminded of John Steinbeck's epic novel "The Grapes of Wrath". At least at the height of the great depression there was some excuse for this kind of tragedy. It seems to me that our Prime Minister is still thinking in terms of the Okies' search for employment in southern California. The Prime Minister has once again evaded the truth. I have personally attempted to get jobs for men in my riding in the north and western parts of Canada, but I have found it virtually impossible to get a local Manpower officer to advise a man whose savings have already been wiped out by a grossly inefficient Unemployment Insurance Commission to head north or west, or anywhere for that matter. The answer I always get is, "He'll likely end up on welfare if he gets stuck out there."
So you see, Mr. Speaker, not only has this government created misery* and hardship for hundreds of thousands of Canadians, but the Prime Minister has attempted to mislead the people on his jaunts across the country. Just last weekend he told an audience in Sturgeon Falls that he

February 28, 1972
Speech from the Throne
was glad he could get out to the people and tell them the truth. Apparently this time around we are to have yet another truth squad. I say to you, some squad; some truth!
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to the horrendous and demoralizing problem hundreds of people in my riding are having with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. First, it is the consensus of people I have talked to that unemployment insurance advertising is misleading on two major points. It is claimed, first, that the waiting period is only two weeks, whereas it can be between three and four weeks after the claimant has applied. Actually, the minimum time that elapses between when the claim is established and the day the claimant's first cheque arrives is five weeks, making a waiting period in some cases of eight or nine weeks.
Let us bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the savings of most people today are exhausted after one month without income. No wonder the tension, no wonder the frustration, no wonder the bitterness engendered by such an inexcusable mess within the Unemployment Insurance Commission! There is only one man responsible for this mess, the man who was given the mandate to establish a "just society"-the Prime Minister.
The other misleading factor is that most people have been led to believe that they will receive increased benefits under the new Unemployment Insurance Act. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that is not entirely accurate. To begin with virtually no claimants qualify for the $100 per week maximum. Secondly, now that benefits are taxable, the average net cheque is virtually no greater than it was under the old act. Moreover, because many claimants fail to qualify for the major attachment requiring a minimum 20-week work period due to the on again-off again employment picture brought about by the government's inane economic policies, their benefits are still very low, averaging $50 per week after taxes. Yet unemployment insurance claimants are being told that the new act provides the greatest unemployment insurance program in the world. Some program!
I would now like to illustrate my condemnation of the de-personalized, computer-oriented Liberal regime by citing specific cases relating to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I received a letter from a constituent, dated February 19, 1972; I will not mention his name. I quote from the letter:
Dear Mr. Blackburn:
I am another of those having trouble with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I was laid off December 3, 1971; all I have received so far is a card every two weeks to send back in and a notice to Claimant stating, "A decision on your claim has not yet been made". The only thing I know is that my claim is dated from December 5, 1971. Also, I was told two weeks ago to expect a cheque within two weeks. As yet none has come. At the moment I have another card to mail back the weekend of the 27th of February. The only people who seem to get any results are those who go to their MPs. It seems that once UIC puts you on the delay circuit they are not able to get you off without help.
Mr. Speaker, I cite another example. A man got in touch with me on February 17, 1972. He applied for benefit and received report cards from last September. He received his first cheque on February 14. I will cite another case. I received a telephone call from a man on January 21, 1972.

He had been laid off the second week of November, 1971. He received a letter saying that all benefits were refused. He received a second letter stating that his claim was established for the 32 weeks at $70 a week. As of January 21, 1972, he had received no benefits. However, in a letter dated January 26, 1972, from the chief of Insurance Operations, Hamilton Unemployment Insurance Commission, I was informed as follows:
The reason for the delay in Mr.-
I will not mention his name.
-claim is that the decision of the insurance officer did not get matched with his payment register in Belleville.
Remember, he had been laid off in November. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is very simple to present this kind of excuse but it is not easy to be the victim of such gross incompetence.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: This government must realize that it is dealing with human beings, not punch-cards in a computer. In concluding this section of my remarks let me cite one more example. I do not wish to overdramatize or emotionalize, but a man came to my home one day in tears: for the previous week he, his wife and young daughter had been living on potatoes and rice, and if it had not been for his $6 baby bonus he would have been forced to go on welfare. It is absolutely repugnant to me that any person who is forced by law to contribute to the unemployment insurance fund should be forced to go to welfare, begging.

speechtext:
Yet the minister responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission had the audacity a few weeks ago to imply that happy days were here again when he said that unemployment insurance claimants could assign their cheques to local welfare agencies. To me, this is simply another example of gross and heartless mismanagement on the part of the government.
I have one more point to make with regard to unemployment insurance. It relates to the shutdown last August of Canadian Westinghouse in the city of Brantford. Severance pay was given to employees at the termination of their employment. This severance pay was given to them in lieu of the pension they would ordinarily have received had they been able to work to the date of their retirement.
Under the present terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act severance pay is, in my opinion, unfairly calculated as earnings. The workers were told that they could not apply for unemployment insurance until the severance pay period had run out. However, several persons I know personally were energetic and aggressive enough to apply for and get a new job within that severance pay period. Two persons in particular were subsequently laid off still within the severance pay period. Deeming their last employer not to be Canadian Westing-house, they applied for unemployment insurance. They began receiving benefits and then subsequently were charged with an overpayment. It being 9.30 o'clock p.m., it is my duty, pursuant to special order made Wednesday, February 23 last, to interrupt these proceedings-more particularly, the hon. member-and put every question necessary to dispose of the amendment now before the House.
The question is on the amendment of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). All those in favour of the amendment will please say yea.
